source_text: CAPUT DECIMUM NONUM, De Dei beatitudine. Hactenus fuit integritas vitae Dei, quae se habet ut virtus: sequitur ea, quae est ut beatitas, et est actus vitae Dei, quo ille perfectione sua infinita per intellectum plene cognita et per voluntatem suam summe amata ita fruitur, ut in ea totus acquiescat. Omnes Deum dicimus beatissimum, quicunque Deum esse confitemur in toto terrarum orbe. Verum enimvero qua in re beatitudo illius consistat, dubitant multi e nostris appetitibus satiati de illius beatitate ratiocinantes.
english: Thus far was the integrity of Gods life, which stands as virtue: there follows that which stands as blessedness, and it is the act of Gods life by which He so enjoys His infinite perfection fully known through the intellect and supremely loved through His will that He wholly rests in it.

All who confess that God is, in the whole circle of the earth, call God most blessed. But in what thing His blessedness consists, many doubt, reasoning about His blessedness from our satiated appetites.

source_text: Machiavellistae nostri temporis beatitudinem ponunt in solo dominatu. Sed errant 1. qui eam in sola potentia et dominio constituunt aut in conservatione sui per potentiam resistentem diu in illa. Nam potentior est equus et leo quam homo, qui tamen iis per sapientiam imperat, et vir fortis sine sapientia non conservatur, ipsique tyranni omnium sunt infelicissimi. Sic enim lapis beatior esset quam aquila aut homo. 2. Neque in sapientia rerum externarum consistit, quia illa fit in nobis non sine praevia passione, et sapiens, si sit impotens, multis est obnoxius miseriis, neque servatur sapientia sua, si bonus non sit, et, quamvis sibi ipsi sit optimus, tamen, si aliquid melius in alio considerat, se non beatum putat, sed invidia fit miser. 3. Neque in sola amoris plena fruitione voluptatum. Qui enim fruitur ignorans et fruitionem non sapit, neque in ea se potest conservare, qui erit beatus? Melior enim est qui scit abundare ac penuriam pati, quam qui abundat sine sensu. 4. Sui quoque amor deficit a beatitate, quando aliquid melius alibi videtur, aut quod amatur non potest aeternari. Itaque qui putant beatitudinem consistere in sola potentia aut sola sapientia aut solo amore aut quovis alio bono privo, omnes errant.
english: The Machiavellians of our time place blessedness in dominion alone. But they err (1) who constitute it in power and dominion alone, or in conservation of oneself by resisting power long in that. For horse and lion are more powerful than man, who yet rules them by wisdom; and a strong man without wisdom is not conserved, and tyrants themselves are of all the most unhappy. Thus a stone would be more blessed than an eagle or a man.

(2) Nor does it consist in wisdom of external things, because that comes about in us not without prior passion; and the wise man, if powerless, is exposed to many miseries, nor is he preserved by his wisdom if he is not good; and though he be best to himself, yet if he considers something better in another, he does not think himself blessed but becomes wretched by envy.

(3) Nor in the sole full enjoyment of pleasures of love. For who enjoys while ignorant and does not taste the enjoyment, nor can conserve himself in it — who will be blessed? Better is he who knows how to abound and to suffer want than he who abounds without sense. (4) Love of self also falls short of blessedness when something better is seen elsewhere, or what is loved cannot be made eternal. Therefore all who think blessedness consists in power alone or wisdom alone or love alone or any other private good err.

source_text: Rectius Boethius finit status omnium bonorum aggregatione perfectum, quae tamen in Deo non aggregantur, sed unum sunt essentialiter, quippe qui omnia potest, scit et amat, adeoque ipse sibi sufficiens est. Si quaeras in quanam harum trium perfectionum beatitudo praecipue consistat: in nulla facile dixeris, sed in tribus aeque. Si tamen una potior censeri debeat, amor erit potior, cujus objectum est bonum, quod formaliter beat; ut autem cognitum, non est bonum. Amor autem praesupponit potentiam et sapientiam, adeoque quasi complet essentiam et beatitudinem. Potentia non supponit sapientiam et amorem: sapientia vero praecedit amorem et ad ipsum quasi ordinatur, quamvis non formaliter, sed radicaliter in potentia insit omnis beatitudo et similiter in sapientia et amore. Incipit quasi in potentia, procedit per sapientiam, consummatur in amore.
english: More rightly Boethius defines the state as perfect by aggregation of all goods, which yet in God are not aggregated but are essentially one, since He can, knows, and loves all things, and so is Himself sufficient to Himself.

If you ask in which of these three perfections blessedness chiefly consists: you will not easily say in any one, but equally in the three. Yet if one ought to be judged more potent, love will be more potent, whose object is the good which formally blesses; but as known it is not the good. Love presupposes power and wisdom, and so as it were completes essence and blessedness.

Power does not suppose wisdom and love: but wisdom precedes love and is as it were ordered to it, although not formally but radically all blessedness is in power and likewise in wisdom and love. It begins as it were in power, proceeds through wisdom, is consummated in love.

source_text: Sed dices, si Deus est beatus, quia omnia potest, scit, amat, videtur non esse perfecte beatus, quia multa odio habet, ut peccata, multaque effugiunt ejus potentiam, quia facta infecta facere nequit. Resp. Beatitudo Dei est ipse Deus, sui amoris objectum adaequatum, et sapientiae et potentiae. Neque enim beatitudo est illi ab extra et accidentalis, ut ait Bernhardus, sed idem est Deo esse et beatum esse. Unde potentia essendi omnia, et scientia sui, quae simul est omnium, faciunt Dei beatitudinem. Posse autem ad extra, quod spectat ad potentiam activam aut passivam, similiterque scire et amare exteriora, non est beatitas essentialis, sed indigentiae effugium et medela, sicut in nobis, qui amamus cibum, uxorem, honorem, quibus conservamur quoniam in nobis et per nos ipsos non possumus conservari. Quapropter non est in nobis idem esse, quod beatum esse. Deus autem non sic, cum perfectionum ipsius infinitas sit absque principio sideriae et indigentia, idemque sit objectum earum, quod ipsae. Dici autem potest, quod Deus ad extra potest omnia, et scit omnia, et amat omnia, dum in se potest esse quod est, et scit se et amat se. Omnia enim participant ejus similitudinem. Dicitur autem Deus quaedam non posse et nescire et nolle, quae vere entia non sunt, ut peccata, contradictiones, privationes, de quibus certum est, quod ista posse, scire et amare, non ex potentia sapientia amore pendeat, sed ex impotentia, insipientia, et, ut sic loquar, disamore, vel horum participio.
english: But you will say: if God is blessed because He can, knows, and loves all things, He seems not perfectly blessed, because He holds many things in hatred, as sins, and many escape His power, because He cannot make what is done undone.

Reply: Gods blessedness is God Himself, the adequate object of His love, and of wisdom and power. For blessedness is not from outside and accidental to Him, as Bernard says, but for God to be and to be blessed are the same. Hence the power of being all things, and the knowledge of Himself which is at once of all things, make Gods blessedness.

But to be able outwardly, as regards active or passive power, and likewise to know and love exterior things, is not essential blessedness but a flight from and remedy of need, as in us who love food, wife, honor, by which we are conserved because we cannot be conserved in ourselves and through ourselves. Therefore in us to be and to be blessed are not the same. But God is not so, since the infinity of His perfections is without beginning of deficiency and need, and their object is the same as they themselves. It can be said that God outwardly can all things, knows all things, and loves all things, while in Himself He can be what He is, and knows Himself and loves Himself. For all things participate His likeness. But God is said not to be able and not to know and not to will certain things which are not truly beings — sins, contradictions, privations — concerning which it is certain that to be able, know, and love those does not hang on power, wisdom, and love, but on impotence, folly, and, so to speak, dislike, or a share of these.

source_text: Est autem beatitudo Dei essentialis proprietas, imo ipsa essentia, quae nulli creaturae communicari potest — Isaia XLII.8; Jerem.; I Cor. XV.28; I Tim. I.11; VI.15; Psal. XVI.2,11. Et est tamen creaturarum intelligentium bonum beatificum ratione objecti destituens actus in objectum tendentis, inque eodem acquiescentis, in quibus duobus creaturae beatitudo consistit ac relucet. Objectum enim est bonum, quo fruimur. Actus vero, quo bono fruimur. Estque gloria aut gaudium. III. Gloria est, qua ob infinitam perfectionem suam omnia excellit. Atque ita hoc attributum est quidem a perfectione Dei, sed cum respectu quodam ad extra, quia excellentiam supra omnia et perfectionem suam infinitam actibus externis varie manifestat — Rom. I.23; IX.5; Psal. VIII; Deut. XXXII; I Tim. I.11; VI.15. Idque vel per luminis splendorisque inusitatam coruscationem et effulgescentiam, vel per oppositam et fissam tenebrositatem, vel per productionem operum, quae ipsius perfectioni et excellentiae congruunt — Matth. XVII.2,5; Luc. II.9; Exod.; Psal. XIX.1.
english: But Gods blessedness is an essential property, indeed the essence itself, which can be communicated to no creature — Isaiah 42:8; Jeremiah; 1 Corinthians 15:28; 1 Timothy 1:11; 6:15; Psalm 16:2,11. And yet it is the beatific good of intelligent creatures by reason of the object completing the act tending into the object and resting in the same, in which two the creatures blessedness consists and shines. For the object is the good which we enjoy. But the act is that by which we enjoy the good.

And it is glory or joy. III. Glory is that by which, on account of His infinite perfection, He excels all things. And so this attribute is indeed from Gods perfection, but with a certain respect outwardly, because He variously manifests His excellence above all things and His infinite perfection by external acts — Romans 1:23; 9:5; Psalm 8; Deuteronomy 32; 1 Timothy 1:11; 6:15.

And that either through unusual flashing and shining of light and splendor, or through opposed and split darkness, or through production of works which agree with His perfection and excellence — Matthew 17:2,5; Luke 2:9; Exodus; Psalm 19:1.

source_text: Manifestum est, Deum non solum esse suammet beatitudinem objective et formaliter, sed etiam omnium rerum objective et effective. Omnia enim modulo quodam suo beantur aliquo bono, imprimis vero creaturae intelligentes, Deus autem est omnis boni causa efficiens et exemplaris, omneque bonum est quaedam illius participatio. Sunt quidem, qui existimant, Deum etiam creaturarum beatitudinem esse formaliter, quia rebus magis est intrinsecus, quam proprius ipsarum actus: sed errant. Deus enim est quidem in nobis, non tamen pars aliqua essentiae aut tota essentia nostra formaliter, sed tantum causaliter et eminenter. Et si vero summum cuique bonum sit proprium esse et conservatio: tamen quia neque sunt, neque conservantur a se, sed a Deo: ideo et beantur ab illo, eumque magis amant, quam sese, dum amant se. Nam non amant solum quod sunt, sed vellent id esse semper et ubique appetuntque infinitatem extensivam et intensivam, quae in solo Deo est, quippe in quo nullus est defectus bonitatis ullus unquam aut uspiam, quae beatitudo vocatur vita aeterna, quam Deus non acquirit aliunde per virtutes suas, sed per eas illam dat aliis. IV. Gaudium est, quo in seipso jucunde fruitur. Hoc non est affectus variabilis. Nam perfecto gaudio Deus afficitur et in se perpetim, ut Lactantii verbo utar, jucundatur — Sophon. III.17. Si philosophum de Dei beatitudine interroges, Aristoteles Stagirites lib. I de caelo cap. IX Deo tribuit vitam sibi ipsi sufficientissimam. Quo dicto nihil verius ab hoc ethnico prolatum est. CAPUT VICESIMUM, De attributis Dei figuratis, sequitur.
english: It is manifest that God is not only His own blessedness objectively and formally, but also of all things objectively and effectively. For all things are blessed in some measure by some good, and especially intelligent creatures; but God is the efficient and exemplar cause of every good, and every good is a certain participation of Him. There are indeed those who think God is also formally the creatures blessedness, because He is more intrinsic to things than their own act: but they err. For God is indeed in us, yet not some part of essence or our whole essence formally, but only causally and eminently.

And if indeed the highest good for each is its own being and conservation: yet because they neither are nor are conserved from themselves but from God: therefore they are also blessed by Him, and love Him more than themselves while they love themselves. For they love not only what they are, but would wish to be that always and everywhere and seek extensive and intensive infinity, which is in God alone, in whom there is never or anywhere any defect of goodness — which blessedness is called eternal life, which God does not acquire from elsewhere by His virtues, but by them gives it to others.

IV. Joy is that by which He pleasantly enjoys Himself. This is not a variable affection. For God is affected with perfect joy and perpetually delights in Himself, to use Lactantius word — Zephaniah 3:17. If you ask a philosopher concerning Gods blessedness, Aristotle of Stagira in On the Heavens book 1 chapter 9 attributes to God a life most sufficient to Himself. Nothing truer than this saying was brought forth by this pagan. CHAPTER TWENTY, On Gods figurative attributes, follows.
